questions.stem: The job of the lexer is to:
options: compute the value of the expression
group the characters of the text into tokens
check that the parentheses are balanced
questions.explanation: Values are the evaluator's job (a), balanced parentheses and the tree the parser's (c, d). The lexer knows nothing about structure.

questions.stem: tokenize("12+3") returns a list of how many tokens?
questions.explanation: ['12', '+', '3']. 12 is one token: the lexer keeps reading while the next character is a digit.

questions.stem: calculate("3 + * 4") fails. Which stage rejects it?
questions.explanation: Every token is valid, so the lexer accepts it (b); but after the +, factor finds *, which cannot start a factor: ValueError: unexpected '*'. Nothing reaches the evaluator (c).

questions.stem: "AST" stands for:
questions.explanation: "Abstract" because it drops the grammar's bookkeeping — the parentheses, and the calls that only passed a value up.

questions.stem: In the grammar, * binds more tightly than + because:
options: the parser keeps a table in which * has the higher number
* is handled in term, a rule that expr is built from
* is always evaluated from right to left
questions.explanation: An expr is a sequence of terms, and every * is consumed inside a term before expr sees the next +; so * ends up deeper in the tree. There is no table (a) — that was shunting-yard.

questions.stem: calculate("2 + 3 * 4 - 1") returns:
questions.explanation: 2 + (3 * 4) - 1 = 13. 19 (a) ignores precedence: ((2 + 3) * 4) - 1.

questions.stem: The root of the AST of 2 * 3 + 4 is:
questions.explanation: (2 * 3) + 4: the last operator applied is the root.

questions.stem: The root of the AST of (1 + 2) * (3 - 4) is:
questions.explanation: Each parenthesised group is a factor of the one term (…) * (…). Parentheses (c) never appear in the tree.

questions.stem: 1 - 2 - 3 evaluates to -4 because subtraction is:
questions.explanation: Left-associative: the leftmost operation first. 1 - (2 - 3) (c) would be 2.

questions.stem: A student writes expr right-recursively: parse a term; if the next token is + or -, return BinOp(op, term, self.expr()). What does it give for 8 - 4 - 2?
questions.explanation: It builds 8 - (4 - 2) = 6: the recursive call parses the whole rest of the line and hangs it on the right. The correct value is 2 (a).

questions.stem: The rule expr := expr '+' term | term is turned directly into a method whose first line is left = self.expr(). On the input 3 it:
options: raises RecursionError — it recurses without consuming a token
loops for ever without using any memory
questions.explanation: expr calls expr at the same position, before reading anything, so no call is ever closer to a base case. Python stops it at its recursion limit, so it does use memory — a frame per call (d is wrong).

questions.stem: In recursive descent, the EBNF repetition ( … )* becomes:
questions.explanation: A while loop that runs while peek() is one of the operators. A rule name becomes a call (a); | becomes an if (c).

questions.stem: Parsing 1 + 2 * 3, how many times is factor called?
questions.explanation: One per number: 1, 2 and 3. (Measured: 3 calls.)

questions.stem: The tree our parser builds for -5 + 2 is:
questions.explanation: Unary minus is a factor, so it binds only the 5: (0 - 5) + 2 = -3. Option (a) is the tree a parser builds if unary minus calls expr instead of factor (W15-B3). The lexer never produces negative numbers (c): -5 is two tokens.

questions.stem: evaluate visits the nodes of the tree in:
options: post-order — both children before the node
questions.explanation: An operator can be applied only once both operand values are known: children first.

questions.stem: The post-order sequence of the AST of (3 + 4) * 2 is:
questions.explanation: Left subtree 3 4 +, right subtree 2, then the root *. It is also the postfix form of Lecture 06.

questions.stem: parse raises ValueError if tokens are left over after expr returns. Without that check:
questions.explanation: expr parses 3 + 4 and stops at the ), which no rule can use; only the final check notices it. (a) and (c) fail inside factor anyway.

questions.stem: Each pair of parentheses costs the parser about three Python frames. With Python's default limit of 1,000 frames, roughly how deeply can calculate nest parentheses?
questions.explanation: 1,000 / 3 is about 333, less a few frames already in use: measured from a script, 329 pairs work and 330 raise RecursionError.

questions.stem: The time of calculate on an expression of n tokens is:
questions.explanation: Each stage touches each token or node a constant number of times.

questions.stem: calculate("1 + 1 + … + 1") with n numbers: how deep does the recursion of evaluate go?
options: about n — the tree leans left all the way down
questions.explanation: The parser uses a loop (a is about the parser), but it builds a tree of height n - 1, and evaluate recurses once per level. log2 n (b) is the balanced case.

questions.stem: When you run a .py file, CPython:
options: interprets the text line by line, with no compilation
compiles it to machine code, like a C compiler
compiles it to bytecode, then interprets the bytecode
questions.explanation: The bytecode is in __pycache__; dis shows it.

questions.stem: Compared with the Week 6 route (shunting-yard, then evaluate_postfix), the main advantage of building a tree is that:
options: the tree can be reused — printed, simplified, compiled — and new grammar rules such as unary minus are easy to add
it needs no memory beyond the tokens
questions.explanation: Both routes are O(n) (a). The tree route needs recursion (c), and memory for the tree (d).

essays.stem: Name the three stages of a translator, with the input and output of each. For each, give an input that it — and only it — rejects, and the exception our calculator raises. How does a compiler differ from an interpreter?
essays.answer:
• Lexer: text → tokens. Rejects characters outside the language: "3 $ 4" → ValueError (unexpected character).
  • Parser: tokens → tree (AST), following the grammar. Rejects valid tokens in an invalid order: "3 + * 4", "(3 + 4", "3 + 4 )" → ValueError.
  • Evaluator: tree → value. Rejects well-formed expressions with no value: "1 / 0" → ZeroDivisionError.
  • Compiler against interpreter: a compiler translates the whole program ahead of time into another program (machine code, bytecode) that runs later; an interpreter executes as it goes and produces the result. Both share the lexer and parser; a compiler replaces the evaluator by a code generator. CPython does both: compile to bytecode, then interpret it.

essays.stem: "Precedence is the shape of the grammar." Explain this sentence using the three rules of our grammar and the tree of 3 + 4 * 2. How do parentheses override precedence? Where would you add a rule for a tighter operator such as ^?
essays.answer:
• expr := term (('+' | '-') term)* — an expression is a sum of terms; term := factor (('*' | '/') factor)* — a term is a product of factors.
  • To parse 3 + 4 * 2, expr splits at + into the terms 3 and 4 * 2; the * is consumed inside the second term. In the tree, * is below +: + over 3 and *(4, 2). Deeper nodes are evaluated first, so * "wins" — value 11.
  • The lower the rule an operator lives in, the tighter it binds: precedence is which rule handles the operator, not a number.
  • Parentheses: factor := '(' expr ')' makes a whole parenthesised expression a factor, the tightest level, so (3 + 4) * 2 puts + below *.
  • A tighter operator such as ^ gets a new rule between term and factor, so that term is built from it and it is built from factors (W15-C5).

essays.stem: What is associativity? Explain why expr must use a loop that makes the tree so far the left child. Describe what goes wrong with a right-recursive expr and with a left-recursive one, with an input for each.
essays.answer:
• Associativity decides how operators of the same precedence group: left-associative 1 - 2 - 3 = (1 - 2) - 3 = -4.
  • The loop in expr does node = BinOp(op, node, self.term()): the tree built so far becomes the left child of each new operator, so the first operation ends up deepest and is evaluated first — left associativity.
  • Right recursion (expr := term ('+' expr)?) puts the recursive result — the whole rest of the line — on the right: 1 - 2 - 3 becomes 1 - (2 - 3) = 2. No error; just a wrong answer, and only for chains of - or / (W15-B1).
  • Left recursion (expr := expr '+' term) calls expr first, with nothing consumed: the recursion makes no progress, and every input, even 3, ends in RecursionError.
  • The ( … )* form with a loop gives left associativity and terminates.

essays.stem: Compare the two routes from infix tokens to a value: shunting-yard plus evaluate_postfix, and Parser plus evaluate. Give their costs, one advantage of each, and the connection between the postfix list and the tree.
essays.answer:
• Stack route: infix_to_postfix (operator stack, precedence table) then evaluate_postfix (value stack). O(n); no recursion, so no depth limit; builds nothing but a list.
  • Tree route: Parser (recursive descent) then evaluate (post-order). O(n) too; the tree can be reused — printed, simplified, compiled — and the grammar is easy to extend (unary minus is one case in factor; the Week 6 infix_to_postfix produces 5 - for -5, which evaluate_postfix rejects). Its recursion depth follows the tree's height.
  • Connection: the postfix list is exactly the post-order traversal of the tree. Shunting-yard emits the post-order of a tree it never builds.

essays.stem: "In a recursive-descent parser, the call stack is the parser's stack." Explain. What decides how deep it grows, and what happens when it grows too deep?
essays.answer:
• Each method call pushes a frame holding its own locals — including its node so far and where it is in its rule. At any moment the frames on the call stack are one path of the parse tree: "inside a factor, inside a term, inside an expr…". Returning pops a frame and resumes the rule that called it. A hand-written parser would need its own explicit stack for this; recursion gets it for free.
  • Depth is set by the shape of the input, not its length: three frames per level of parentheses (expr, term, factor); a flat chain 1 + 1 + … is a loop and adds nothing to the parser's depth (but see W15-K2 for evaluate).
  • Too deep: Python's limit (1,000 frames by default) raises RecursionError — at about 330 nested pairs of parentheses. Real compilers raise the limit, or use an explicit stack for deep cases.
